content:
A non-retractable foreskin can be completely normal in babies and young boys. However, phimosis can become a medical problem when the foreskin is scarred, causes pain, repeatedly cracks or becomes inflamed, interferes with urination or causes problems during erections or sexual activity.

At Beverley Clinic in North-West London, we assess and treat children, teenagers and adults with tight foreskins and phimosis.

Treatment depends on the patient's age, symptoms, appearance of the foreskin and the underlying cause. Circumcision can provide a definitive surgical treatment for troublesome phimosis.

When the foreskin is sufficiently mobile, it can be gently pulled backwards to expose the glans.

Phimosis is when the opening of the foreskin is too tight to retract comfortably over the glans.

There is an important difference, however, between a young child's foreskin that has not naturally become retractable yet and a foreskin that has become abnormally tight because of scarring or disease.

This distinction is important because the two situations should not automatically be treated in the same way.

The foreskin is naturally attached to the glans during early childhood and gradually separates as the child grows. Some boys become fully retractable relatively early, while for others this process takes considerably longer.

Parents should not forcibly retract a child's foreskin simply because it does not pull back.

Forceful retraction can cause pain, small tears and subsequent scarring.

A child's foreskin therefore needs to be assessed in the context of his age, symptoms and the appearance of the foreskin, rather than deciding that he has phimosis simply because it cannot yet be pulled back.

Common symptoms can include:

  • Difficulty retracting the foreskin
  • Inability to retract the foreskin
  • A visibly tight ring at the opening of the foreskin
  • Pain when trying to retract the foreskin
  • Cracking or splitting of the foreskin
  • Bleeding following small tears
  • Recurrent redness or inflammation
  • Recurrent balanitis
  • Difficulty cleaning underneath the foreskin
  • Ballooning of the foreskin when passing urine
  • A weak or altered urinary stream in more severe cases
  • Pain or tightness during erections
  • Pain during sexual activity
  • Difficulty using a condom comfortably
  • The foreskin becoming progressively tighter
  • White, pale or scarred areas of foreskin

The presence of one of these symptoms does not automatically mean circumcision is necessary.

An examination helps establish why the foreskin is tight and what treatment is most appropriate.

New or progressively worsening phimosis in an adult deserves assessment, particularly if there is visible scarring, whitening, recurrent cracking, inflammation or another change in the skin.

One possible cause is BXO / lichen sclerosus.

Other skin conditions, infection, inflammation and repeated trauma can also affect the foreskin.

If you previously had a normally retractable foreskin and it has become increasingly tight, do not assume this is simply part of ageing.

What does phimosis feel like during an erection?

Some men can retract their foreskin when the penis is soft but find that it becomes tight or painful when erect.

The foreskin may feel as though there is a tight band around the penis, or it may retract partly and then become uncomfortable.

This can cause pain during masturbation or sexual intercourse and may result in small tears or bleeding.

It is important to distinguish this from a short or tight frenulum, which can produce similar pulling or discomfort but may require a different treatment.

There is also an important complication to understand called paraphimosis.

Phimosis versus paraphimosis

The names sound similar but they describe different problems.

Phimosis means the foreskin is too tight to retract normally over the glans.

Paraphimosis occurs when a tight foreskin has been pulled backwards behind the glans and then cannot be brought forward again.

The trapped foreskin can form a constricting band and the glans may become increasingly swollen and painful.

This is important because the aim is not simply to remove some foreskin for cosmetic reasons. The procedure is being performed to treat a specific medical problem.

Before circumcision we examine:

  • Where the tight band is located
  • How much foreskin is affected
  • Whether there is visible scarring
  • Whether BXO is suspected
  • The amount and mobility of penile skin
  • The frenulum
  • The position of the penis and surrounding tissue
  • Whether there has been previous surgery

We then plan the circumcision so that the problematic tight area is appropriately treated while retaining enough healthy mobile skin for comfortable healing and erections.

What are the risks of circumcision for phimosis?

Circumcision is a surgical procedure and complications can occur. Potential problems include:

  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • Swelling
  • Bruising
  • Wound separation
  • Delayed healing
  • Scarring
  • Altered sensation
  • Cosmetic dissatisfaction
  • Need for further treatment

Your penis will permanently look and feel different after removal of the foreskin.

We discuss the relevant risks before treatment so that you can make an informed decision.

Phimosis assessment and circumcision in London

If you experience pain, cracking, difficulty retracting or uncomfortable erections and are considering treatment, contact Beverley Clinic.

We can assess your foreskin and determine whether there is associated scarring, lichen sclerosus / BXO, a tight frenulum or another condition that needs to be considered when planning your treatment.
